cpuset is a threaded controller on 7.1.3: kernel/cgroup/cpuset.c line 3675 '.threaded = true,' (also in github torvalds/linux v7.1) and cgroup-v2.rst lines 410-416 'Currently, the following controllers are threaded ... cpu, cpuset, perf_event, pids'. So the no-reboot path could in principle keep Jeremy's one-process layout by putting only the pass thread into an isolated child partition of a threaded subtree; the docs say nothing about partition roots inside threaded subtrees, so this needs one root-level test (mkdir, cgroup.type=threaded, cpuset.cpus.partition=isolated, read back the partition file) before it is offered.

After isolcpus=domain, init is moved to the housekeeping CPUs: kernel/sched/core.c lines 8838-8840 '/* Move init over to a non-isolated CPU */ if (set_cpus_allowed_ptr(current, housekeeping_cpumask(HK_TYPE_DOMAIN)) < 0) BUG();'. Every process then inherits Cpus_allowed 0-125 (variant A) unless it sets affinity itself. Jeremy's ev3-churn-job.sh already runs the label under 'taskset -c 120-127' (phoenix-crb-round3.txt '=== runs_and_checks ===') and the root cpuset keeps cpuset.cpus.effective 0-127 ('=== cgroups ==='), so the job still reaches 126-127. Post-reboot checks to add: 'grep Cpus_allowed_list /proc/1/status' expects 0-125, and 'taskset -c 127 true' as positron-perf must succeed.

A non-per-CPU kernel thread is allowed on the target CPUs: rcu_exp_par_gp_kthread_worker/8 has Cpus_allowed_list 112-127 (host read-only /proc/<pid>/status on 2026-10-22; the inspection '=== background ===' '--- rcu kernel threads' lists /1 0-15 ... /4 48-63 with the same 16-CPU pattern). Whether isolcpus=domain narrows that mask is not shown by the evidence files. Add to the post-reboot list: the Cpus_allowed_list and psr of rcu_exp_par_gp_kthread_worker/8 (expect 112-125 only on the NO_HZ_FULL kernel). Workqueue rescuers, by contrast, are bound to wq_unbound_cpumask (workqueue.c 5729-5733) and leave 126-127 after the reboot.

The vendor headers match upstream for the isolation core: /usr/src/linux-headers-7.1.3-.../include/linux/sched/isolation.h has md5 ec35c927f2df010c99ea4fd5180a5e07 and 92 lines, identical to the analyst's upstream v7.1.3 copy, and the vendor headers' Makefile reads VERSION = 7, PATCHLEVEL = 1, SUBLEVEL = 3 (host read-only check). The analyst's isolation.c and Makefile copies also match github torvalds/linux v7.1 line for line in the quoted places, so the kernel-source quotes in K1-K3, K7, K8, K14 are trustworthy for the vendor build's header-level interface; the vendor .c files remain unseen.

Two clean post-reboot signals the analyst used but did not justify: /sys/devices/system/cpu/housekeeping prints the nohz_full housekeeping mask only when HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE is enabled and an empty line otherwise (drivers/base/cpu.c 303-314), so '0-125' there is the single cleanest NO_HZ_FULL check for P4; and 'workqueue: Restricting unbound_cpumask (...) with %s (...) leaves no CPU, ignoring' is printed only when the restriction would empty the mask (workqueue.c 7919-7925), so an empty grep is a valid pass.

isolcpus flag parsing on 7.1.3 (isolation.c 314-367): an unknown alphabetic flag is skipped with 'isolcpus: Skipped unknown flag %.*s' (357), a flag containing a non-letter makes the handler return 0 with 'isolcpus: Invalid flag' (352-355) and the whole isolcpus= is then listed under 'Unknown kernel command line parameters', and a bad CPU list prints 'Housekeeping: nohz_full= or isolcpus= incorrect CPU range' (221). The planned string 'isolcpus=domain,managed_irq,126-127' parses as intended; the dmesg grep in K14 ('Housekeeping|isolcpus|Unknown kernel command line') covers all three failure messages.

'Broken broadcast TLBI completion' is the v7.1.3 desc of ARM64_WORKAROUND_REPEAT_TLBI (cpu_errata.c 724-730) and its CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4118414 list (343-366) ends with MIDR_ALL_VERSIONS(MIDR_NEOVERSE_V3AE); v6.8's desc is 'Qualcomm erratum 1009, or ARM erratum 1286807, 2441009' (v68 cpu_errata.c 520-521). MIDR 0x410fd832 decodes to part 0xd83 = ARM_CPU_PART_NEOVERSE_V3AE (cputype.h line 95), r0p2, matching lscpu. Host /boot/config-6.8.0-147-generic has CONFIG_ARM64_WORKAROUND_REPEAT_TLBI=y (line 401), CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4118414=y (420), CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_3194386=y (419), and the 6.8.0-147 headers define ARM_CPU_PART_NEOVERSE_V3AE 0xD83 (cputype.h line 96). Ubuntu's 6.8.0-147.147 changelog shows the backports: under 'linux (6.8.0-103.103)' the lines '- arm64: cputype: Add Neoverse-V3AE definitions' and '- arm64: errata: Apply workarounds for Neoverse-V3AE'; under 'linux (6.8.0-146.146)' the lines '- arm64: errata: Mitigate TLBI errata on various Arm CPUs' and '- [Config] Enable CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4118414' (CVE-2025-10263 // CVE-2026-53354). So the stock kernel carries the same upstream TLBI patch; the exact list could not be read (Launchpad HTTP 403 for WebFetch and curl). Corrections: (1) the two 'vendor-only errata' are not a runtime difference on this board: CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4311569 is applied only when the early_param 'arm_si_l1_workaround_4311569' is given (cpu_errata.c 145-166, comment 'its safe to have the workaround off by default'); the host cmdline has no such parameter and dmesg has no 'Enabling cache maintenance workaround for ARM SI-L1 erratum 4311569' line, so it is inactive on the vendor kernel too; CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4193714 matches only C1-Pro r0p0-r1p2 with SME (cpu_errata.c 952-962, '.midr_range = MIDR_RANGE(MIDR_C1_PRO, 0, 0, 1, 2)'), not V3AE. (2) 'certainly lacks' the GIC quirk should read 'upstream has no such quirk; the Ubuntu tree was not readable (HTTP 403)'. (3) Stock config differences re-checked on the host: CONFIG_HZ=1000 (line 460), CONFIG_PREEMPT_VOLUNTARY=y (119) with CONFIG_PREEMPT_DYNAMIC=y (123), CONFIG_CPU_FREQ_DEFAULT_GOV_ONDEMAND=y (635), CONFIG_ACPI_CPPC_CPUFREQ=m (650). Conclusion (vendor kernel stays plan of record; stock never booted here per wtmp) stands, but the silicon-risk argument now rests only on the vendor GIC quirk and the untested status.
verdicts.correction: The stock 6.8.0-147 kernel has never booted on this board and lacks the vendor-only GIC 'AGI CPU A0' quirk (absent from upstream v6.8 and v7.1.3; Ubuntu tree unverified). The 'Broken broadcast TLBI completion' workaround (ARM64_WORKAROUND_REPEAT_TLBI via CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4118414, V3AE in the v7.1.3 list) is upstream code that Ubuntu backported in 6.8.0-146.146 together with the Neoverse-V3AE definitions (6.8.0-103.103), so it is very likely present in the stock kernel. The two vendor-only config options are not a runtime difference here: 4311569 is off unless 'arm_si_l1_workaround_4311569' is on the command line (it is not), and 4193714 applies only to C1-Pro CPUs. Remaining differences are HZ 1000, PREEMPT_DYNAMIC/voluntary and the ondemand default governor.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed parts: cpuset.c 1341-1361 (cpuset_update_sd_hk_unlock: 'if (update_housekeeping) { ... WARN_ON_ONCE(housekeeping_update(isolated_hk_cpus));') and isolation.c 121-163 (housekeeping_update replaces the HK_TYPE_DOMAIN mask and calls workqueue_unbound_housekeeping_update(), tmigr_isolated_exclude_cpumask(), kthreads_update_housekeeping()); base-cpu.c 293-294 ('isolated' uses HK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOT, so a partition never shows there and churn.py's core_isolated stays false); cgroup-v2.rst 2655-2659 ('isolated state without any load balancing from the scheduler and excluded from the unbound workqueues. Tasks placed in such a partition with multiple CPUs should be carefully distributed and bound to each of the individual CPUs'), 2616-2618, 583-586 (common-ancestor rule, which blocks the unprivileged account); host state (subtree_control 'cpu memory pids', cpuset.cpus.isolated empty) re-checked 2026-10-22. Corrections: (1) cpuset is a threaded controller (cgroup-v2.rst 410-416: 'the following controllers are threaded ... cpu, cpuset, perf_event, pids') and cpuset.c carries no partition restriction for threaded cgroups (the only 'threaded' token is '.threaded = true' at line 3675), so 'a process cannot straddle a partition and its parent' is not a hard rule: a threaded subtree with the pass thread alone in a child 'isolated' partition (cpuset.cpus=127) under a parent 'root' partition (120-127) is allowed by the documented rules; untested on this host. (2) The recipe's AllowedCPUs=0-127 on system.slice/user.slice is safe on 7.1.3: cpus_excl_conflict() (665-678) only compares cpuset.cpus.exclusive values and a superset test when exclusive_cpus changes, and compute_excpus()/rm_siblings_excl_cpus() (1434-1443, 1386-1423) subtract only siblings' exclusive or effective-exclusive CPUs; on 6.7-6.12-era kernels (validate_change compared user_xcpus = cpuset.cpus of siblings) the same recipe would yield 'isolated invalid (Cpu list in cpuset.cpus not exclusive)', which matters only for the stock 6.8 kernel. (3) prstate_housekeeping_conflict() (1322-1332): once isolcpus=domain is in force after the P2 reboot, CPUs outside HK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOT can only be used in an 'isolated' partition, never 'root'. (4) After the partition is created, every task outside it has its allowed set cut to 0-119 (cgroup-v2.rst 2616-2618), so Jeremy's 'taskset -c 120-127' from his own SSH session fails with EINVAL until root moves his shell into the partition, as the action already requires.
verdicts.correction: A cgroup v2 'isolated' partition works without reboot on 7.1.3 and updates the HK_TYPE_DOMAIN housekeeping mask (workqueues, kthreads, timer migration), but gives no tick stop, no RCU offload, no managed-IRQ steering, never appears in /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated (so churn.py records core_isolated=false and the perf lane refuses the host), and cannot be entered by positron-perf. Jeremy's one-process layout is reproducible in principle through a threaded subtree (cpuset is a threaded controller), but this is untested; the simpler statement is that his current taskset/placement only works after root moves the job shell into the partition. The sibling AllowedCPUs=0-127 settings do not invalidate the partition on this kernel.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed mechanism: systemd v255 src/shared/cgroup-setup.c cg_enable_everywhere() lines 940-995 opens '<path>/cgroup.subtree_control' and, for every supported v2 controller, writes '+name' if it is in the mask and '-name' otherwise ('s[0] = FLAGS_SET(mask, bit) ? '+' : '-'), tolerating only EBUSY on disable; src/core/cgroup.c unit_update_cgroup() lines 2518-2527 calls it with enable_mask and stores cgroup_enabled_mask; unit_get_enable_mask() lines 2219-2232 = members mask & supported; unit_realize_cgroup_now_enable() lines 2814-2842 recurses to the parent slice up to the root slice. Host: systemd 255 (255.4-1ubuntu8.18), no AllowedCPUs/CPUAffinity in unit files (inspection '=== cgroups ===' 'systemd AllowedCPUs in config:' empty). Correction on the trigger: 'cgroup-realized', 'cgroup-realized-mask', 'cgroup-enabled-mask' are serialized and deserialized across daemon-reload/daemon-reexec (src/core/unit-serialize.c), and unit_realize_cgroup_now_enable() returns early when 'unit_has_mask_enables_realized()' holds (lines 2835-2836), so a reload or reexec by itself does not rewrite the root's cgroup.subtree_control. The '-cpuset' write happens at the next realization of the root slice with a changed enable mask: the first unit or 'systemctl set-property' that needs a controller not yet enabled at the root, or a property change on -.slice. Against a leaf child partition the '-cpuset' write succeeds (EBUSY only when a deeper cgroup has it enabled), which offlines the cpuset css of the partition. The mitigation (an AllowedCPUs= property so cpuset is in systemd's own members mask) is right. Code reading only; not exercised on the host.
verdicts.correction: systemd 255 has no setting for cpuset.cpus.partition. It rewrites the root cgroup.subtree_control with '-' for every controller none of its units needs whenever it re-realizes the root slice with a changed controller set (not on a plain daemon-reload, whose realized masks are serialized); a hand-enabled cpuset controller then disappears and dissolves a hand-made partition unless some unit uses AllowedCPUs=.

extra_findings: E1 (changes the K10 action for variant A): with isolcpus=domain,managed_irq,126-127 and Jeremy's unchanged 'taskset -c 120-127', churn.py's placement() gives the non-pass threads the mask 120-126 (job CPUs minus the siblings of 127; phoenix-crb-round5.txt lines 1140-1169), which includes the isolated CPU 126. Kernel placement rules: a task whose current CPU is outside a new affinity mask is moved to cpumask_any_and_distribute() over the mask (kernel/sched/core.c 3127-3138, a rotating pick that can return 126), a task whose current CPU is inside the mask is not moved (core.c 2926-2934), a task forked on a domain-isolated CPU is placed on that same CPU (fair.c 8829-8894 with no domains, select_idle_sibling 8117/8187-8189), and no load balancer ever pulls tasks off a domain-isolated CPU. So in an estimated 1 of 7 runs (the distribute pick) plus the runs where the taskset'd shell itself lands on 126, the harness and all its unpinned threads sit on CPU 126 with no balancing, giving bimodal results. Fix: run the churn job with 'taskset -c 120-125,127' (job CPUs exclude the spare isolated CPU) or isolate 127 only. The perf lane is unaffected: records.py choose_cores() builds its taskset list from housekeeping cores plus the pass core (phoenix-crb-round5.txt lines 398-404).

E2 (K12/P4): UEFI Secure Boot is disabled: /sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-8be4df61-93ca-11d2-aa0d-00e098032b8c reads '6 0 0 0 0' (attribute bytes then value 0) and /sys/kernel/security/lockdown is absent (host read-only check 2026-10-22). A self-built unsigned kernel and its modules boot without MOK enrollment; the vendor .deb kernel booting today is consistent with this.

E3 (K6/P4): NO_HZ_FULL is a member of the Kconfig choice 'Timer tick handling' with HZ_PERIODIC and NO_HZ_IDLE (kernel/time/Kconfig lines 110-159, 'default NO_HZ_IDLE if NO_HZ'); enabling it means disabling NO_HZ_IDLE ('scripts/config --disable NO_HZ_IDLE --enable NO_HZ_FULL; make olddefconfig') and the resulting .config must show '# CONFIG_NO_HZ_IDLE is not set'.

E4 (K14/P2 verification): a post-reboot 'dmesg | grep isolcpus' always matches the '[ 0.000000] Kernel command line: ...' line (phoenix-crb-followup.txt '=== dmesg_greps ===' and host dmesg today), so a 'must print nothing' check has to exclude that line.

E5 (K8/P1c): cpuset is a threaded controller in 7.1.3 (Documentation/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.rst lines 410-416: 'cpu, cpuset, perf_event, pids') and kernel/cgroup/cpuset.c has no partition restriction for threaded cgroups (only '.threaded = true' at line 3675), so one process can in principle keep its pass thread in a child 'isolated' partition and its workers in the parent partition through a threaded subtree; untested here and it still does not populate /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated. Version note: on 7.1.3 sibling cpuset.cpus overlap no longer invalidates a partition (cpus_excl_conflict, cpuset.c 665-678, compares only cpuset.cpus.exclusive), whereas 6.7-6.12-era kernels compared siblings' cpuset.cpus and would report 'isolated invalid (Cpu list in cpuset.cpus not exclusive)' for the K8 recipe; relevant only if the stock 6.8 kernel were ever used.

E6 (K5/F4): the two vendor-only errata options are not a runtime difference on this board. CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4311569 is applied only when the early_param 'arm_si_l1_workaround_4311569' is on the command line (arch/arm64/kernel/cpu_errata.c lines 145-166, comment 'its safe to have the workaround off by default'); the host cmdline lacks it and dmesg has no 'Enabling cache maintenance workaround for ARM SI-L1 erratum 4311569' line, so it is inactive on the vendor kernel. CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4193714 matches only C1-Pro r0p0-r1p2 with SME (cpu_errata.c 952-962). The Ubuntu 6.8.0-147.147 changelog shows the V3AE definitions and workarounds backported in 6.8.0-103.103 and 'arm64: errata: Mitigate TLBI errata on various Arm CPUs' with '[Config] Enable CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4118414' in 6.8.0-146.146 (scratchpad/verify/ubuntu-src/changelog.txt lines 3489-4425, 12792-14497), and /boot/config-6.8.0-147-generic has CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_4118414=y (line 420) and CONFIG_ARM64_ERRATUM_3194386=y (line 419). The stock-kernel risk argument therefore rests on the vendor GIC 'AGI CPU A0' quirk and the never-booted status, not on the errata config diff.

E7 (K9/P1c): systemd 255 serializes 'cgroup-realized', 'cgroup-realized-mask' and 'cgroup-enabled-mask' across daemon-reload/daemon-reexec (src/core/unit-serialize.c), and unit_realize_cgroup_now_enable() returns early when the enable mask is already realized (src/core/cgroup.c lines 2835-2836), so the root cgroup.subtree_control is rewritten (with '-cpuset') only when the root slice is next realized with a changed enable mask, for example the first unit or set-property needing a controller not yet enabled at the root. The AllowedCPUs= guard in K8/K9 remains the right mitigation; test it after setup with a harmless 'systemctl set-property --runtime <some other slice> IOAccounting=yes' rather than daemon-reload.

E8 (K8, after P2): once isolcpus=domain is in force, cpuset's prstate_housekeeping_conflict() (kernel/cgroup/cpuset.c lines 1322-1332: 'CPUs outside of HK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOT, if defined, can only be used in an isolated partition') makes any 'root' partition that includes 126-127 invalid; only 'isolated' partitions may contain boot-isolated CPUs.

E9 (clock dimension, confirmed line): on a NO_HZ_FULL kernel sched_tick() calls arch_scale_freq_tick() only 'if (housekeeping_cpu(cpu, HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE))' (kernel/sched/core.c lines 5652-5653), so the AMU-derived frequency scale of nohz_full CPUs 126-127 is not refreshed by the tick; CPPC feedback_ctrs deltas read directly from the registers stay valid, while scaling_cur_freq/cpuinfo_avg_freq for those CPUs should be treated as suspect after P4.

E10 (D2/F19): Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt lines 2739-2740 mark isolcpus= '[Deprecated - use cpusets instead]' and lines 2763-2765 say domain isolation by isolcpus 'is irreversible', while the SDK gates read /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated, which reflects only boot-time isolcpus (drivers/base/cpu.c lines 293-294, HK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOT). The SDK tooling therefore forces the boot-parameter route; no cpuset-based setup can satisfy churn.py or records.py without an SDK change.

E11 (K7, minor): nohz_full CPUs remain in the timer-migration hierarchy and are treated as idle when their tick stops, while domain-isolated CPUs are excluded from it (kernel/time/timer_migration.c lines 447-452); with the vendor config's CONFIG_PM_SLEEP_SMP=y a boot CPU listed in nohz_full= would be cleared with 'NO_HZ: Clearing %d from nohz_full range for timekeeping' (tick-sched.c 668-677), which the proposed sets avoid by excluding CPU 0.

findings.dimension: CPU CLOCK AND CPUFREQ (cppc_cpufreq, schedutil vs performance, boost, persistence, root-free clock measurement, H1 fake-device lateness, WFI wake-up, thermal risk, acceptance rule)

findings.claim: Each of the 128 CPUs is its own cppc_cpufreq policy under schedutil with a 1000 us rate limit; 'boost' is absent rather than disabled (CPPC highest_perf == nominal_perf == 140, so the driver reports no boost capability and cpuinfo_max_freq is the nominal 2.8 GHz), and the 'performance' governor means one standing request of desired_perf 140 = 2800 MHz per selected CPU (1 perf unit = 20 MHz, offset 0).
findings.evidence: phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === cpufreq ===: 'governors: 128 schedutil; drivers: 128 cppc_cpufreq; ... global boost: 0 policy120 boost: 0 related/affected 120: 120 / 120 transition_latency: 0 ... highest_perf=140 lowest_freq=1600 lowest_nonlinear_perf=80 lowest_perf=80 nominal_freq=2800 nominal_perf=140 reference_perf=50'. Host read (this check): /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/schedutil/rate_limit_us = 1000 (a global tunable; the per-policy dir the inspection looked for does not exist because cppc_cpufreq has no per-policy governor flag); 'cpupower -c 120 frequency-info': 'boost state support: Active: no', 'maximum transition latency: Cannot determine or is not supported.' Kernel source drivers/cpufreq/cppc_cpufreq.c (master): 'if (caps->highest_perf > caps->nominal_perf)' / 'policy->boost_supported = true;' and 'policy->cpuinfo.max_freq = cppc_perf_to_khz(caps, policy->boost_enabled ? caps->highest_perf : caps->nominal_perf)'. drivers/acpi/cppc_acpi.c cppc_perf_to_khz: linear map with slope (nominal_freq-lowest_freq)/(nominal_perf-lowest_perf) = (2800-1600)/(140-80) = 20 MHz per unit and offset nominal_freq - nominal_perf*slope = 0, so 80 -> 1,600,000 kHz and 140 -> 2,800,000 kHz. Documentation/admin-guide/pm/cpufreq.rst, performance governor: 'causes the highest frequency, within the scaling_max_freq policy limit, to be requested for that policy', requested once when the governor is set and again when limits change.
findings.implication: Jeremy's 'no boost' needs no action and cannot be changed on this board. 'Performance' on CPUs 120-127 is exact (single-CPU policies) and costs nothing on the other CPUs. The firmware (SCP) can still deliver less than the request; that is visible only through the feedback counters (C4). The schedutil rate limit (1000 us) is longer than the fake device's 100 us spin window, so no governor action can ever help inside that window.
findings.action: No action beyond C2. Record in the hand-off: 'boost: not available (highest_perf = nominal_perf = 140); scaling_max_freq = cpuinfo_max_freq = 2800000 kHz = nominal'.

findings.claim: The live governor change is a root sysfs write per policy (or one cpupower command, which works with the vendor kernel), takes effect at once, needs no reboot, and can target exactly CPUs 120-127 or all 128.
findings.evidence: phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === cpufreq ===: '-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 4096 Oct 21 18:31 /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy120/scaling_governor' (root-only write), 'avail governors: ondemand userspace performance schedutil', 'related/affected 120: 120 / 120'; phoenix-crb-followup.txt === cpufreq_extra ===: 'freqdomain_cpus: perms=444 value=120'. phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === tools ===: 'cpupower /usr/bin/cpupower' and package 'linux-tools 7.1.3-arm-agi-20260916-v0.7.2-g4dbc8bb88858'; host read: 'cpupower -c 120 frequency-info' printed the policy (so the cpupower build matches the running kernel).
findings.implication: P1a can be done any time by the admin account without a reboot; the 120-127-only variant is the recommended one (C8).
findings.action: As arm, 120-127 only:  for c in $(seq 120 127); do echo performance | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy$c/scaling_governor >/dev/null; done   (equivalent: sudo cpupower -c 120-127 frequency-set -g performance).  All 128:  for p in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*; do echo performance | sudo tee $p/scaling_governor >/dev/null; done   (equivalent: sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance).  Verify as any user:  cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy12[0-7]/scaling_governor | sort | uniq -c   -> '8 performance';  cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy12[0-7]/scaling_cur_freq | sort | uniq -c   -> '8 2800000' (this is the request, not a measurement; the delivered check is in C4/C9).  Revert: the same loops with 'schedutil'.

findings.claim: A live governor change survives nothing but is reverted by nothing on this host except a reboot or a human; for persistence, the boot parameter cpufreq.default_governor=performance does apply to the modular cppc_cpufreq driver (the built-in cpufreq core stores the name and applies it when each policy is created at driver probe, and the performance governor is built in), but it is host-wide; a 120-127-only setting needs a small systemd oneshot unit; the packaged cpupower.service (disabled, empty config) is a host-wide no-reboot alternative.
findings.evidence: Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt: 'cpufreq.default_governor= [CPU_FREQ] Name of the default cpufreq governor or policy to use. This governor must be registered in the kernel before the cpufreq driver probes.' drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq.c (master): 'static char default_governor[CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN];', 'module_param_string(default_governor, default_governor, CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN, 0444);', and in cpufreq_init_policy(): governor = get_governor(policy->last_governor) if set, else 'gov = get_governor(default_governor);', else cpufreq_default_governor(); cpufreq_core_init(): 'if (!strlen(default_governor))' 'strscpy(default_governor, gov->name, CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN);'. Documentation/admin-guide/pm/cpufreq.rst (CPU Initialization): a new policy gets 'the default scaling governor determined by the kernel command line or configuration, but it may be changed later via sysfs'. Host: /sys/module/cpufreq/parameters/default_governor currently reads 'schedutil' (the parameter file exists, 0444); phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === kernel_config ===: 'CONFIG_CPU_FREQ_GOV_PERFORMANCE=y' (built in, so registered before the module probes), 'CONFIG_ACPI_CPPC_CPUFREQ=m'; cppc_cpufreq.c has 'MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(acpi, cppc_acpi_ids);' (udev autoload). Revert sources checked: phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === background ===: 'tuned=inactive power-profiles-daemon=inactive thermald=inactive cpupower=inactive cpufrequtils=inactive ondemand=inactive' and 'tuned=not-found power-profiles-daemon=not-found ... cpufrequtils=not-found ondemand=not-found'; host read: 'systemctl list-unit-files' -> 'cpupower.service disabled enabled' with /etc/cpupower-service.conf fully commented ('#GOVERNOR=...'), /usr/libexec/cpupower runs 'cpupower frequency-set ${GOVERNOR:+ -g "$GOVERNOR"}' on all CPUs; /etc/udev/rules.d is empty; 'grep -rl scaling_governor /etc' -> only /etc/cpupower-service.conf, /etc/cpufreq-bench.conf, an apparmor abstraction. CPU hotplug does not revert: cpufreq.c __cpufreq_offline(): 'strscpy(policy->last_governor, policy->governor->name,' and cpufreq_init_policy restores it. Jeremy's tools only read: ~/positron/runs/isol.py lines 61,70,71,127 use rd() on scaling_governor/scaling_cur_freq; tools/perf/host_facts.sh is 'Read-only' per its header.
findings.implication: S5 holds. Choose the persistence path by scope: host-wide -> kernel parameter (no race, rides with the isolcpus reboot) or cpupower.service (no reboot, but no ordering after the module load); 120-127 only -> custom unit. Until a persistent path is in place, every reboot silently returns all CPUs to schedutil, so the pre-run checklist must include the governor check.
findings.action:
Host-wide + reboot: add 'cpufreq.default_governor=performance' to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in the new drop-in, update-grub, reboot; verify: grep -o 'cpufreq.default_governor=[a-z]*' /proc/cmdline; cat /sys/module/cpufreq/parameters/default_governor (expect performance); cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*/scaling_governor | sort | uniq -c (expect '128 performance').  Host-wide, no reboot, persistent:  sudo sed -i "s/^#GOVERNOR=.*/GOVERNOR='performance'/" /etc/cpupower-service.conf && sudo systemctl enable --now cpupower.service && systemctl status cpupower.service   (check the status after every boot: the unit is not ordered after the cppc_cpufreq module load).  120-127 only, persistent (file /etc/systemd/system/positron-cpufreq.service):  [Unit]
Description=Positron: performance cpufreq governor on CPUs 120-127
[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 60); do [ -e /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy127/scaling_governor ] && break; sleep 1; done; for c in $(seq 120 127); do echo performance > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy$c/scaling_governor; done; grep -H . /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy12[0-7]/scaling_governor'
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target   then  sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now positron-cpufreq.service.  Rollback of any path: systemctl disable --now the unit, or remove the parameter and update-grub, then the schedutil loop from C2.

findings.claim: The root-free clock measurement is sound, with four corrections: the formula is exactly the kernel's; the draft's 3 s arithmetic is right (139.78 units = 2795.5 MHz); but (a) the reference counter advances at 1000 MHz only while the core is not idle (it stops in WFI), so delta(ref)/wall is the non-idle fraction and the ratio is the clock during active time; (b) every read of feedback_ctrs or cpuinfo_cur_freq from another CPU sends the target CPU IPIs (2 per feedback_ctrs read, 4 per cpuinfo_cur_freq read); (c) scaling_cur_freq (isol.py's cur_khz) is the last request, never a measurement; (d) perf stat cycles:u / task-clock gives the clock the thread itself saw, without IPIs or root.
findings.evidence: Documentation/admin-guide/acpi/cppc_sysfs.rst: 'delivered_counter_delta = fbc_t2[del] - fbc_t1[del]', 'reference_counter_delta = fbc_t2[ref] - fbc_t1[ref]', 'delivered_perf = (reference_perf x delivered_counter_delta) / reference_counter_delta'. phoenix-crb-followup.txt === cpufreq_extra ===: 'delta ref=3004523060 delta del=8399236187 wall=3.01s' -> 50 x 8399236187 / 3004523060 = 139.78 units (file: '139.8 units -> est. 2796 MHz'), 3004523060 / 3.0069 s = 999.2 MHz (file: 'reference counter rate est. 999.2 MHz'); the printed 'idle cpu121 before: fb=ref:12050540980 del:28483309657' differs from the pair used in the arithmetic by ref +3012 / del +5359 because followup.sh lines 20-21 read fb 121 twice (each read wakes the CPU for about 3 us). Reference counter stops when idle (host reads this check): idle CPU 123, 1 s apart: 'ref:18809439400' -> 'ref:18809580644' -> 'ref:18809612608' (+141,244 and +31,964 ticks per second = 0.01-0.014 % of the 1e9 a free-running 1 GHz counter would add); CPU 120 'ref:5794573760' at uptime 106,669 s (a free-running counter would read about 1.07e14); busy CPU 125, 0.25 s windows: 'ref +253947020 (1000 MHz active-rate, active 100%)'. IPIs: arch/arm64/kernel/topology.c cpc_read_ffh() -> counters_read_on_cpu(): 'return smp_call_function_single(cpu, func, val, 1);' (one call per counter); cppc_cpufreq.c cppc_get_perf_ctrs_sample(): two cppc_get_perf_ctrs() calls with 'udelay(2); /* 2usec delay between sampling */' (so cpuinfo_cur_freq = 4 IPIs); dmesg: 'CPU features: detected: Activity Monitors Unit (AMU) on CPU0-127'. scaling_cur_freq = request: cpufreq.rst: scaling_cur_freq is 'the frequency of the last P-state requested by the scaling driver from the hardware' and 'may or may not reflect the frequency the CPU is actually running at'; cppc_cpufreq_set_target: 'freqs.new = target_freq;'; the host kernel config has no CONFIG_CPUFREQ_ARCH_CUR_FREQ line; observed requests 1750000, 1758203, 1711718, 1873046 kHz are not multiples of the 20,000 kHz perf step, i.e. schedutil arithmetic (1.25 x 2800 MHz x util/1024, util about 512 for a freshly forked task: kernel/sched/fair.c post_init_entity_util_avg 'long cap = (long)(cpu_scale - cfs_rq->avg.util_avg) / 2;'). cpuinfo_avg_freq: topology.c '#define AMU_SAMPLE_EXP_MS 20', returns -EAGAIN when the tick sample is stale and no non-idle CPU shares the policy (single-CPU policies here), hence 'Resource temporarily unavailable' on idle CPUs and 2797265 kHz on the busy one. perf stat as user (phoenix-crb-followup.txt === perf_rt_checks ===: 'cycles:u ... instructions:u' counted; kernel.perf_event_paranoid = 2): this check, hiccup spin mode on CPU 126: '10,566,326,477 cycles:u' over '3,789.34 msec task-clock:u' = 2.788 GHz, matching feedback counters 139.6 units = 2792 MHz over the same 3.79 s. Ratio bias on mostly-idle CPUs: idle window 'ref +70692 ... delivered est. 1411 MHz' and 'cpuinfo_avg_freq ... avg=1451953' on idle CPU 121 (below the 1.6 GHz floor).
findings.implication: For proof of a fixed clock: read feedback_ctrs from CPU 0 only at run boundaries (2 IPIs per CPU per snapshot), require delta(ref) >= 1e8 ticks (0.1 s of active time) before trusting a ratio, and use 'perf stat -e task-clock,cycles:u' around the thread of interest for a per-thread number. Never cite scaling_cur_freq or isol.py's cur_khz as the delivered clock; the isol.py 5 s sampler reads only scaling_cur_freq (no IPI), so it does not perturb the run.
findings.action: Use this recipe (any user): C=127; F=/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu$C/acpi_cppc/feedback_ctrs; A=$(taskset -c 0 cat $F); <run>; B=$(taskset -c 0 cat $F); units = 50 * (del_B-del_A)/(ref_B-ref_A); MHz = 20 * units; active_fraction = (ref_B-ref_A)/(1e9 * wall_s).  Per thread: perf stat -e task-clock,cycles:u <command>  -> GHz = cycles:u / task-clock (a lower bound when the thread spends time in the kernel). Ask Jeremy to add the two feedback_ctrs snapshots (before/after, from CPU 0) to isol.py snap next to cur_khz.

findings.claim: Measured on the host now: under schedutil a spinning thread reaches a 2.8 GHz request within about 14 ms and a delivered 2.8 GHz within about 25 ms (est. from 10 ms windows), but a thread with the fake device's sleep-then-spin pattern (about 3 % duty) keeps a 1.6 GHz request and an effective active-time clock of 1.39-1.45 GHz, i.e. 1.9-2.0 times slower than the 2.79 GHz a spinning thread gets.
findings.evidence: This check, 10 ms ramp trace on CPU 126 (spin launched at about t = 200 ms): 't 211 ms window 14 ms active 91 % delivered 2200 MHz requested 2756 MHz', 't 225 ms ... 2773 / 2800', 't 239 ms ... 2800 / 2800' and 2800/2800 for every later window; 0.25 s trace on CPU 125: first window 2783 MHz, then 2800 MHz x11. hiccup sleep mode on idle CPU 125 (2000 cycles, 3.79 s, schedutil): feedback counters 'delta ref=107914760 del=155476299 wall=3.79s active=2.8% delivered perf=72.0 units = 1441 MHz during active time'; perf stat: '136,593,199 cycles:u' over '98.14 msec task-clock:u' (user 0.0942 s, sys 0.0043 s) = 1.39 GHz (1.45 GHz against user time only). hiccup spin mode: 139.6 units = 2792 MHz and 2.788 GHz by perf. Jeremy's samples: phoenix-crb-round4.txt === freq_files ===: 'freq.sleep.txt: 89 1600000 1 1711718', 'freq.spin.txt: 75 2800000 14 1600000 1 1873046' (requests). kernel/sched/cpufreq_schedutil.c: 'next_freq = C * max_freq * util / max', 'Take C = 1.25 for the frequency tipping point at (util / max) = 0.8' -> a 3 % duty task maps to about 170 MHz, clamped to the 1.6 GHz policy minimum; rate limit 1000 us (host read).
findings.implication: Under schedutil the fake device thread (null_timing.cpp 'kSpinNs = 100'000'), any idle reader's CPU and every wake-up path run at 1.4-1.6 GHz; the pass thread (76 % busy in churn-r1) already runs at 2.8 GHz most of the time. The performance governor therefore changes the mostly-idle threads and the wake-up paths, not the busy pass loop. Whether the 1.39-1.45 GHz figure is a real post-WFI clock effect or a counter/accounting bias at idle edges is not decided (both methods have a low bias on a mostly-idle CPU); the same hiccup sleep-mode measurement under 'performance' decides it (expect about 140 units / 2.79 GHz if there is no bias).
findings.action: Repeat after the governor change: perf stat -e task-clock,cycles:u ~/positron/runs/hiccup/hiccup 125 2000 sleep (about 4 s), plus the feedback_ctrs pair from C4; record both numbers in the hand-off as 'sleeping thread: 1.39-1.45 GHz (schedutil) vs X GHz (performance)'.

findings.claim: H1 (the 1.6 GHz sleep-pattern clock causes the fake device's lateness) is not supported as a sufficient cause: Jeremy's own probe of that pattern on an idle CPU under schedutil shows mean lateness 0.02-0.03 us and zero cycles over the 2.5 us band; the record is voided on late_mean (6.2 us) versus the band, not on late_max; the device thread is unpinned and shared CPUs 120-126 with the workers and client (1.3k-7.7k interrupts/s per CPU during churn-r1) and sleeps with the default 50 us timer slack, which eats half of its 100 us spin margin. The governor will shorten each interruption and the retire path by up to about 1.9 times but will not remove them.
findings.evidence: This check, ~/positron/runs/hiccup/hiccup 125 2000 sleep (idle CPU, schedutil): 'lateness n=2000 mean=0.03 p50=0.02 p90=0.04 p99=0.05 max=2.1 us; >2.5us 0 >50us 0 >90us 0', 'spin stall ... max=4.8 us; >2.5us 8', 'wake overshoot n=2000 mean=52.73 p50=52.88 p90=53.49 p99=54.29 max=59.6 us; >2.5us 2000 >50us 1981' (second run: lateness max 0.1 us, stall max 9.8 us >2.5us 19, overshoot mean 53.49 max 61.0 us); spin mode: lateness mean 0.01 us, stall max 5.6-10.7 us. hiccup.c (full read): usage 'hiccup CPU CYCLES MODE', pins itself with sched_setaffinity, period 1.2-2.6 ms, 'nanosleep until (next - 100 us) [like FakeDevice::run], then spin'. Timer slack: /proc/self/timerslack_ns = 50000 for a positron-perf process; kernel/time/hrtimer.c hrtimer_nanosleep: 'hrtimer_set_expires_range_ns(&t.timer, rqtp, current->timer_slack_ns);'; the SDK already fixes this for one thread: runtime/events/waker.h:26 'inline constexpr std::chrono::nanoseconds kWakerTimerSlack{1000};  // 1 us, 2% of the period' and waker.cpp:51 '::prctl(PR_SET_TIMERSLACK, ...)', but grep finds prctl nowhere else (not in backends/null_timing). Device thread placement: fake_device.cpp:113 'thread_ = std::thread([this] { run(); });' with no affinity call in backends/null_timing (phoenix-crb-round5.txt: the only affinity calls are pass_loop.cpp:37 and worker_thread.cpp:17); churn.py placement(): 'every other thread of the runs on this job's other CPUs' (120-126). Void rule: backends/null_timing/pass_log.cpp:417-420 'out.lateness_band_s = kLatenessBand * *shortest_cohort;' ... 'out.void_run = late_mean > *out.lateness_band_s;'; docs/null-timing.md:87 'lateness_band_s, 0.2% of the shortest cohort period'. churn-r1: phoenix-crb-round3.txt === runs_and_checks === r1-run.rec_bind.check.txt: "device {'retired': 37284, 'late_mean_s': 6.246e-06, 'late_max_s': 0.000220151, 'lateness_band_s': 2.502e-06, 'void': True}"; phoenix-crb-round4.txt === churn_r1_job_log ===: '"irqs_each_watch": {"120": 255378, "121": 277078, "122": 1133890, "123": 885004, "124": 1324691, "125": 222394, "126": 871614, "127": 40859}', '"irqs_cpus_0_119": 70209', '"seconds": 172.9' (1.3k-7.7k interrupts/s on the shared CPUs versus 236/s on the pass CPU); 'busy_share_each_watch': 122: 0.1214, 123: 0.0829, 127: 0.7609. The recorded lateness includes the retire path: fake_device.cpp:273-284 retire() does write(hemi) if pending and completions_.try_push(...) before 'late = std::max(0, clock_.now_ns() - entry.retire_ns)'.
findings.implication: Expect P2's re-run of ev3-churn-job.sh after the governor change to lower late_mean (the device's retire path and every interruption run faster) but not necessarily below 2.5 us; the lever that the data points to is on Jeremy's side: give the fake device thread its own CPU (e.g. 126, with the pass thread on 127 and workers/client on 120-125) and set PR_SET_TIMERSLACK to 1 us in FakeDevice::run as the waker does. Both need no root. This changes D3's CPU map.

findings.claim: With no cpuidle driver the CPUs idle in plain WFI (dsb + wfi), so waking a waiting reader costs an IPI, the WFI exit and the scheduler path with no firmware (PSCI) call and no deep-state exit latency; the measured hrtimer wake-up latency on an idle CPU at the schedutil floor is about 2.7 us mean, 4.3 us p99, 10-11 us max (est.: wake overshoot minus the 50 us slack), and it will run at 2.8 GHz instead of 1.4-1.6 GHz under 'performance'; the arch timer event stream (100 us) matters only for WFE-based waits.
findings.evidence: phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === cpufreq === '--- cpuidle' 'driver: none governor: menu available: menu' and no state* files; host read: /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuidle/current_driver = 'none'; dmesg: 'cpuidle: using governor menu' and no idle-state line; === kernel_config ===: 'CONFIG_CPU_IDLE=y', 'CONFIG_ARM_PSCI_CPUIDLE=y' (built, not registered), 'CONFIG_ARM_ARCH_TIMER_EVTSTREAM=y'; lscpu flags include 'evtstrm'. arch/arm64/kernel/idle.c: arch_cpu_idle() is 'our default idle handler' and calls cpu_do_idle(), whose default path is 'dsb(sy);' then 'wfi();'. dmesg: 'psci: PSCIv1.1 detected in firmware' (PSCI is used for CPU bring-up; idle never calls it without a cpuidle driver). include/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.h: '#define ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US 100'. hiccup wake overshoot (idle CPU, schedutil): mean 52.73 us, p99 54.29 us, max 59.6 us and 53.49 / 55.83 / 61.0 us; minus the 50,000 ns slack -> 2.7 us mean, 4.3-5.8 us p99, 9.6-11 us max; 19-30 of 2000 overshoots were below 50 us (the timer was expired early by another interrupt).
findings.implication: For Jeremy's 'waking a waiting reader' metric the governor change is the direct lever (the idle reader's CPU otherwise sits at the floor); nothing needs changing in PSCI or the event stream, and the absence of deeper idle states is favourable. The GIC erratum workaround ('GICv3: Arm AGI CPU A0 detected, enabling GIC erratum workaround') is an unknown cost on every interrupt that only a before/after measurement can show.

Recommendation: 120-127 only, host-wide only per window after a calibration.

findings.claim: Evidence for Jeremy and an acceptance rule: the clock is 'fixed' for a counted run when, for each CPU in 120-127 with at least 0.1 s of active time, the feedback-counter ratio over the run is 139.0-140.0 units (2780-2800 MHz), the governor reads 'performance' and the request 2800000 kHz before and after, boost is 0 with scaling_max_freq 2800000 kHz, and the harness's own cycles:u / task-clock (if Jeremy accepts a perf stat wrapper) is at least 2.75 GHz; mostly-idle CPUs are judged by governor and request until the calibration shows whether the counter ratio stays near 140 under 'performance'.

Confirmed: the sleep-then-spin pattern keeps a 1.6 GHz request (freq.sleep.txt) and measures an effective active-time clock of 1.39-1.45 GHz (feedback counters and perf stat, this check). verdicts.reason: The sleep-pattern numbers reproduce: hiccup 125 2000 sleep under schedutil on an idle CPU gave feedback delta ref 109,469,568 ticks and delta del 158,848,545 over 3.855 s wall, so 72.55 units = 1,451 MHz during active time at 2.84 % active; perf stat gave 136,729,627 cycles:u over 98.29 ms task-clock:u = 1.391 GHz (1.450 GHz against 94.3 ms user time). Spin mode: 2.786 GHz by perf, 139.39 units by counters. Jeremy's freq files are quoted exactly (phoenix-crb-round4.txt === freq_files ===). kernel/sched/cpufreq_schedutil.c:180 'next_freq = C * max_freq * util / max' and :187 'Take C = 1.25 for the frequency tipping point at (util / max) = 0.8.' exact. The ramp claim is NOT reproduced: a spin arriving on idle CPU 124 after a 0.2 s sleep, sampled in 8.8 ms windows from CPU 0, kept a 1,600,000 kHz request for its first 35 ms at 100 % activity, then 1,750,000 kHz at about 40 ms, then 1,905,859 / 2,064,453 / 2,299,609 / 2,441,796 / 2,578,515 / 2,709,765 kHz, and 2,800,000 kHz at about 100 ms after the spin started; delivered clock was 1,553-1,600 MHz for the first 45 ms and 2,791 MHz or more from about 110 ms. That is the PELT ramp (32 ms half-life) from near-zero utilization. The analyst's 14 ms is consistent only with a thread forked from a busy parent, which inherits the parent's utilization share (fair.c post_init_entity_util_avg). Arithmetic slip: 3 % duty gives 1.25 x 2800 MHz x 0.03 = 105 MHz (185 MHz at the nominal 5.3 % duty of 100 us per 1.9 ms), not 170 MHz; both clamp to the 1.6 GHz floor, so the conclusion stands.
verdicts.correction: Replace 'reaches a 2.8 GHz request within about 14 ms and a delivered 2.8 GHz within about 25 ms' with 'reaches a 2.8 GHz request between 14 ms (a thread forked from a busy parent, analyst's trace) and about 100 ms (a thread that arrives after a sleep, this check) after it starts spinning, with the delivered clock at 2.79 GHz or more about 10 ms after the request; the ramp follows PELT utilization with a 32 ms half-life'. extra_findings: The schedutil ramp time depends on the thread's starting PELT utilization, which the analyst did not state: a spin arriving on idle CPU 124 after a 0.2 s sleep kept a 1,600,000 kHz request for its first 35 ms, got 1,750,000 kHz at about 40 ms and 2,800,000 kHz at about 100 ms, with delivered 2,791 MHz or more from about 110 ms (verify-clock/ramp124.txt, 8.8 ms windows sampled from CPU 0; v7.1 kernel/sched/fair.c:1321 for the start value, cpufreq_schedutil.c:180,187 for the mapping). For the SDK this means every pass-thread idle gap long enough to decay utilization is followed by a 1.6 to 2.8 GHz ramp of up to about 100 ms under schedutil.

Under schedutil during churn-r1 the pass CPU's request was not steady: ~/positron/runs/churn-r1/isol.samples.jsonl (34 samples, 5.1 s apart, 168 s) has CPU 127 at 2,800,000 kHz in 26 of 34 samples and 1,600,000 kHz in 6 of 34 (plus 1,750,000 and 2,783,593 kHz once each); CPUs 120-126 sat at 1,600,000 kHz in 29-34 of 34 samples each. These are requests (scaling_cur_freq), so they show the governor's behaviour, not the delivered clock (host read 2026-10-22 01:20 UTC).

The 250 Hz tick keeps running on the fake device thread's CPU: v7.1 kernel/time/tick-sched.c:979 'if (delta <= (u64)TICK_NSEC)' keeps the tick when the next timer is within one 4 ms jiffy, and the device's sleeps are 1.2-2.6 ms, so NO_HZ_IDLE gives that CPU no relief; only nohz_full on a rebuilt kernel would, and only with one runnable task. This also explains the 19-30 of 2,000 hiccup sleeps that ended before the 50 us slack (expected 2,000 x 50 us / 4000 us = 25).

The CPPC reference counter runs at exactly the 1000 MHz arch timer rate while the core is active: hiccup spin on CPU 126 advanced ref by 3,789,125,468 ticks over 3.788 s of task-clock (999.96 MHz). In sleep mode the ref delta (109.5e6 ticks = 2.84 % of 3.855 s) exceeds the thread's own task-clock (98.3 ms = 2.55 %); the 0.29 % difference is kernel time on that CPU (wake-up path, ticks, IPIs). So delta(ref)/wall measures the CPU's non-idle fraction, not the thread's run time (host 2026-10-22 01:15 UTC).

cpuinfo_avg_freq on mostly idle CPUs reads below the 1.6 GHz floor: CPU 120 read 1,400,000 kHz at 01:17 UTC (host), CPU 121 read 1,451,953 kHz in phoenix-crb-followup.txt === cpufreq_extra ===, CPUs 124-127 read 1,591,406-1,599,609 kHz. With the feedback-counter ratio (72.5 units = 1,451 MHz) and perf (1.391 GHz) this is the third independent method that shows a sub-floor effective clock at idle edges; whether it is a real post-WFI clock effect or counter accounting stays undecided (the analyst's open question).

The sysfs modification time 'Oct 21 18:31' on policy120/scaling_governor (phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === cpufreq ===) should not be read as a governor write at 18:31: sysfs (kernfs) file times reflect when the inode was instantiated, and cpuinfo_cur_freq in the same directory shows 'Oct 21 21:08'; 18:31-18:32 UTC is when Jeremy's isol.py snap first read these files (phoenix-crb-round4.txt === isol_before_summary === time_utc 2026-10-21T18:32:09Z). Not verified from kernfs source in this check.

The acpi_power_meter driver is not built in the vendor kernel ('# CONFIG_SENSORS_ACPI_POWER is not set'; 'modinfo: ERROR: Module acpi_power_meter not found'), so the ACPI000D:00 power meter (status 15, no driver) cannot be read without a kernel build; C8's optional action is impossible as written (host 2026-10-22 01:17 UTC).

ThreadWait::sleep_ns is std::this_thread::sleep_for (backends/null_timing/fake_device.cpp:63), so the fake device's sleep goes through nanosleep and gets the thread's 50 us timer slack; with the measured 53 us wake overshoot the 100 us spin window (kSpinNs) is effectively about 47 us. The waker thread is the only thread that sets a 1 us slack (waker.cpp:51).

cpupower's 'current CPU frequency: 1.75 GHz (asserted by call to kernel)' (host, CPU 120, 01:13 UTC) is the scaling_cur_freq request of a freshly forked task (1.25 x 2800 MHz x 0.5), another example that tools reporting from scaling_cur_freq show requests, not measurements.

The hiccup stall statistics separate the two clocks cleanly: at 2.79 GHz (spin mode) p99 stall 1.60 us with 1 of 2,000 windows over 2.5 us; at 1.45 GHz (sleep mode) 18 of 2,000 over 2.5 us with max 5.9 us; the maximum stall (8.0 us in spin mode this check, 10.7 us in the analyst's) does not scale with the clock, so the governor removes the typical tick cost from the 2.5 us band but not the rare 8-11 us events (host 2026-10-22 01:15 UTC).

verdicts.reason: Boost: drivers/cpufreq/cppc_cpufreq.c (master) sets 'policy->boost_supported = true;' only under 'if (caps->highest_perf > caps->nominal_perf)', and cpuinfo.max_freq is 'cppc_perf_to_khz(caps, policy->boost_enabled ? highest_perf : nominal_perf)'; with highest_perf = nominal_perf = 140 (phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === cpufreq === 'highest_perf=140 ... nominal_perf=140') boost is not supported, and cpufreq.c store_local_boost returns -EINVAL when '!policy->boost_supported', so it cannot be enabled. Perf unit: cppc_acpi.c cppc_perf_to_khz() uses 'mul = caps->nominal_freq - caps->lowest_freq; div = caps->nominal_perf - caps->lowest_perf; mul *= KHZ_PER_MHZ; offset = caps->nominal_freq * KHZ_PER_MHZ - div64_u64(caps->nominal_perf * mul, div); retval = offset + div64_u64(perf * mul, div)' -> (2800-1600)*1000/(140-80) = 20,000 kHz per unit, offset = 2,800,000 - 140*20,000 = 0, so 80 -> 1,600,000 kHz and 140 -> 2,800,000 kHz. Governor: cpufreq.rst says the performance governor 'causes the highest frequency, within the scaling_max_freq policy limit, to be requested for that policy', requested when selected and when limits change; cpufreq.c cpufreq_start_governor() calls governor->start then governor->limits. Rate limit: kernel/sched/cpufreq_schedutil.c sugov_init 'tunables->rate_limit_us = cpufreq_policy_transition_delay_us(policy);' and the tunables kobject parent is get_governor_parent_kobj(policy), which is cpufreq_global_kobject unless the driver sets CPUFREQ_HAVE_GOVERNOR_PER_POLICY; cppc_cpufreq_driver.flags = 'CPUFREQ_CONST_LOOPS | CPUFREQ_NEED_UPDATE_LIMITS' (no per-policy flag), so the tunable is the global /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/schedutil/rate_limit_us, which this check read as 1000 (mode 644 root). cpufreq.c cpufreq_policy_transition_delay_us() returns policy->transition_delay_us if set, else 'latency + (latency >> 1)' from cpuinfo.transition_latency, else 'return USEC_PER_MSEC;' = 1000 us. One precision: the driver never assigns policy->cpuinfo.transition_latency (absent in cpu_init in master), so the host's 'cpuinfo_transition_latency=0' means 'not provided', and cpupower prints 'Cannot determine or is not supported' for it; the 1000 us comes from the USEC_PER_MSEC fallback because cppc_get_transition_latency() returns 0 for a desired-perf register in SystemMemory/SystemIO ('If desired_reg is in the SystemMemory or SystemIo ACPI address space, then assume there is no latency.' ... 'return 0;'). Sugov rate limit semantics: sugov_should_update_freq() returns 'delta_ns >= sg_policy->freq_update_delay_ns' (bypassed only on limits_changed/need_freq_update), so no frequency update inside a 100 us window after the previous one.

verdicts.reason: Kernel-parameter path confirmed from source: kernel-parameters.txt 'cpufreq.default_governor= [CPU_FREQ] Name of the default cpufreq governor or policy to use. This governor must be registered in the kernel before the cpufreq driver probes.'; cpufreq.c has 'static char default_governor[CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN];' and 'module_param_string(default_governor, default_governor, CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN, 0444);' (hence the 0444 file /sys/module/cpufreq/parameters/default_governor, host read 'schedutil'); cpufreq_init_policy() tries get_governor(policy->last_governor), then get_governor(default_governor), then cpufreq_default_governor(), and ends with 'ret = cpufreq_set_policy(policy, gov, pol);'; cpufreq_core_init() does 'if (!strlen(default_governor)) strscpy(default_governor, gov->name, CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN);'. The performance governor is built in (CONFIG_CPU_FREQ_GOV_PERFORMANCE=y) and cppc_cpufreq is a module with 'MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(acpi, cppc_acpi_ids);', so the parameter applies at every policy's creation, host-wide. Hotplug does not revert: __cpufreq_offline() does 'strscpy(policy->last_governor, policy->governor->name, CPUFREQ_NAME_LEN);'. The custom oneshot unit is valid under systemd 255: substitution applies only to '${FOO}' and to '$FOO' as a separate word ('Use "${FOO}" as part of a word, or as a word of its own' / 'Use "$FOO" as a separate word on the command line'), and the unit's $(seq ...), $i and $c sit inside one single-quoted word, so they reach /bin/sh unchanged ('To pass a literal dollar sign, use "$$"' is the safer spelling). cpupower.service text confirmed on the host and upstream (cpupower.service.in: Type=oneshot, EnvironmentFile=-/etc/cpupower-service.conf, ExecStart=/usr/libexec/cpupower, RemainAfterExit=yes, WantedBy=multi-user.target, no After= ordering), and /usr/libexec/cpupower runs 'cpupower frequency-set ${GOVERNOR:+ -g "$GOVERNOR"}' on all CPUs. BUT that unit file, the helper script, /usr/bin/cpupower and libcpupower.so are all owned by positron-perf (see C2), so enabling cpupower.service would make root execute files the test account can edit at every boot.
verdicts.correction: Persistence options that stand: (1) host-wide via cpufreq.default_governor=performance on the kernel command line (reboot), (2) CPUs 120-127 only via the custom positron-cpufreq.service oneshot unit (write $$ for each $ or ship the loop as a root-owned script). Drop the cpupower.service option until the admin has chown'ed the vendor linux-tools files to root:root; after that it is a valid host-wide no-reboot path with the ordering caveat the finding states. Also note: the vendor package, not Ubuntu, supplies cpupower.service (Ubuntu's linux-tools does not ship it).

verdicts.reason: Formula: cppc_sysfs.rst 'delivered_counter_delta = fbc_t2[del] - fbc_t1[del]', 'reference_counter_delta = fbc_t2[ref] - fbc_t1[ref]', 'delivered_perf = (reference_perf x delivered_counter_delta) / reference_counter_delta', and cppc_acpi.c show_feedback_ctrs prints 'ref:%llu del:%llu\n'. (a) Counters stop in idle: Documentation/arch/arm64/amu.rst 'Constant counter: increments at the fixed frequency of the system clock.' and 'When in WFI or WFE these counters do not increment.'; host re-check: idle CPU 123 ref advanced +125,568 ticks in 1.0 s from CPU 0 (0.013 % of the 1e9 a free-running 1 GHz counter would add). (b) IPIs: cppc_acpi.c cpc_read() 'if (reg->space_id == ACPI_ADR_SPACE_FIXED_HARDWARE) return cpc_read_ffh(cpu, reg, val);', arch/arm64/kernel/topology.c cpc_read_ffh() reads the core or const counter through counters_read_on_cpu(), which calls smp_call_function_single() when IRQs are enabled (local read only when IRQs are off); cppc_get_perf_ctrs() reads DELIVERED_CTR and REFERENCE_CTR (CTR_WRAP_TIME only 'if (CPC_SUPPORTED(ctr_wrap_reg))', and wraparound_time = U64_MAX here means unsupported) -> 2 IPIs per read from another CPU; cppc_cpufreq_get_rate() samples twice with 'udelay(2); /* 2usec delay between sampling */' -> 4 IPIs, and cpuinfo_cur_freq is 'cpufreq_freq_attr_ro_perm(cpuinfo_cur_freq, 0400)' (root only). (c) scaling_cur_freq: cpufreq.c show_scaling_cur_freq() uses 'freq = IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_CPUFREQ_ARCH_CUR_FREQ) ? arch_freq_get_on_cpu(policy->cpu) : 0;' and otherwise 'policy->cur' (the setpolicy branch does not apply to cppc_cpufreq); CONFIG_CPUFREQ_ARCH_CUR_FREQ is defined only in drivers/cpufreq/Kconfig.x86 (absent from drivers/cpufreq/Kconfig), so on arm64 it is never offered and scaling_cur_freq is the last requested target; cppc_cpufreq_set_target sets 'freqs.new = target_freq', and the driver quantizes the request with cppc_khz_to_perf ('retval = offset + div64_u64(freq * mul, div)', truncating), so 1,758,203 kHz is 87 units = 1,740 MHz at the firmware. cpufreq.rst: scaling_cur_freq 'is the frequency of the last P-state requested by the scaling driver from the hardware' which 'may or may not reflect the frequency the CPU is actually running at'. cpuinfo_avg_freq: topology.c '#define AMU_SAMPLE_EXP_MS 20', arch_freq_get_on_cpu() returns -EAGAIN when the sample is stale and no non-idle CPU shares the policy ('No alternative to pull info from'); cpufreq.rst: on ARM an idle CPU returns EAGAIN. (d) perf stat cycles:u / task-clock: perf_event_paranoid=2 allows user-only counting (phoenix-crb-followup.txt === perf_rt_checks === 'cycles:u' counted). Minor note: the fresh-fork 1,750,000 kHz requests are explained by kernel/sched/fair.c post_init_entity_util_avg 'long cap = (long)(cpu_scale - cfs_rq->avg.util_avg) / 2;' (util 512 -> 1.25 x 512/1024 x 2,800 MHz = 1,750 MHz).

Note the AMU documentation only states that the counters do not increment in WFI/WFE; it says nothing about the clock in the first microseconds after WFI exit, so the proposed re-measurement under 'performance' is the right discriminator for the floor-frequency hypothesis, and the perf-stat ratio (PMU cycles over scheduler-clock time, user-mode only) is the method less exposed to AMU idle-edge accounting.

verdicts.reason: Linux parts hold. Default slack: init/init_task.c '.timer_slack_ns = 50000, /* 50 usec default slack */' (host: /proc/self/timerslack_ns = 50000). nanosleep uses it: kernel/time/hrtimer.c hrtimer_nanosleep() 'hrtimer_set_expires_range_ns(&t.timer, rqtp, current->timer_slack_ns);' (master passes the slack directly; RT/DL tasks get HRTIMER_MODE_HARD in __hrtimer_setup_sleeper instead, irrelevant here because rtprio is 0). A slack timer is not run before its soft expiry (__hrtimer_run_queues breaks on 'basenow < hrtimer_get_softexpires(timer)') and the hardware event is programmed for the hard expiry, so the thread normally wakes about 50 us plus wake-up latency after the requested time unless another interrupt lands in between, which matches the measured 52.7-53.5 us mean overshoot. PR_SET_TIMERSLACK: kernel/sys.c has no capability check; 'if (arg2 <= 0)' restores the default, else 'current->timer_slack_ns = arg2;'; it is per thread (current) and a no-op for RT/DL policies, so FakeDevice::run must call it on its own thread, which needs no privilege. The SDK facts (fake_device.cpp lines, waker.h:26, pass_log.cpp void rule, churn.py placement) and the churn-r1 numbers are outside this lens and were not re-read; not a Linux semantics claim.

verdicts.reason: The acceptance thresholds (139.0-140.0 units, >= 0.1 s active time, >= 2.75 GHz by perf stat) are a policy proposal, not a Linux behaviour; Jeremy decides. Semantics behind it: the 20 MHz-per-unit step is the OS-side linear map of cppc_perf_to_khz (confirmed in C1); whether the SCP firmware actually changes frequency in 20 MHz steps is insufficient data (the SCMI performance-domain OPP list would show it; it is under debugfs, root only). Two semantics facts qualify the rule: (1) on the current kernel the per-policy cpuinfo_avg_freq (0444) is an IPI-free delivered-clock read for a busy CPU (last tick sample, 20 ms expiry) but returns EAGAIN or an idle-biased value on an idle CPU (host reads: EAGAIN, 1,451,953 kHz, 1,476,562 kHz on idle policy120); (2) on a future nohz_full kernel, arch_freq_get_on_cpu() never uses a non-housekeeping CPU's own sample ('if (!housekeeping_cpu(cpu, HK_TYPE_TICK) || time_is_before_jiffies(...))') and with single-CPU policies finds no other CPU, so it returns -EAGAIN always for CPUs 120-127; the feedback_ctrs pair (2 IPIs per read) or perf stat must carry the rule then.

schedutil on this host runs in fast-switch mode: there are no 'sugov:N' kthreads (ps -eo comm | grep -c ^sugov -> 0). kernel/sched/cpufreq_schedutil.c sugov_kthread_create() returns early when policy->fast_switch_enabled, and cppc_cpufreq sets policy->fast_switch_possible = cppc_allow_fast_switch(policy->cpus), which is true only when the desired/min/max perf registers are writable SystemMemory or SystemIO registers; frequency changes are therefore plain memory writes from scheduler context (sugov_update_single_freq -> cpufreq_driver_fast_switch), not SCHED_DEADLINE kthread wake-ups on CPUs 120-127. Consequence for the plan: switching to 'performance' removes the per-tick governor computation and the variable request, but there is no sugov kthread or PCC mailbox round-trip to remove on the isolated CPUs. Also the CPPC FIE kworker 'cppc_fie' does not exist here (counters are FFH/AMU, not PCC; fie_disabled=0), and drivers/base/arch_topology.c topology_set_scale_freq_source() keeps the AMU source ('/* Use ARCH provided counters whenever possible */'), so frequency invariance is the tick-local AMU read with no IPIs. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/kernel/sched/cpufreq_schedutil.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/acpi/cppc_acpi.c (cppc_allow_fast_switch) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/base/arch_topology.c ; host: /sys/module/cppc_cpufreq/parameters/fie_disabled = 0, no cppc_fie or sugov in /proc/*/comm]

cpuinfo_avg_freq (0444, world readable) is an IPI-free delivered-clock read for a BUSY CPU on the current kernel: arch/arm64/kernel/topology.c arch_freq_get_on_cpu() returns (scale * arch_scale_freq_ref(cpu)) >> SCHED_CAPACITY_SHIFT from the AMU sample taken at the last scheduler tick ('#define AMU_SAMPLE_EXP_MS 20'); with HZ=250 the sample is at most 4 ms old on a busy CPU. It returns -EAGAIN (or an idle-biased value such as 1,476,562 kHz) on an idle CPU. On a nohz_full kernel (plan P4) the function never uses a non-housekeeping CPU's own sample ('if (!housekeeping_cpu(cpu, HK_TYPE_TICK) || time_is_before_jiffies(last_update + msecs_to_jiffies(AMU_SAMPLE_EXP_MS)))') and with single-CPU policies finds no sibling ('No alternative to pull info from' -> -EAGAIN), so on CPUs 120-127 it will always fail after P4; the acceptance rule must then rely on feedback_ctrs (2 IPIs per read, read only at run boundaries) or perf stat. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/arch/arm64/kernel/topology.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq.c (show_cpuinfo_avg_freq) ; host: cpuinfo_avg_freq on idle policy120 -> 1476562 this check, EAGAIN and 2797265 after a spin in phoenix-crb-followup.txt === cpufreq_extra ===]

scaling_cur_freq on arm64 is the raw governor target, not the quantized firmware request: cpufreq.c show_scaling_cur_freq() uses arch_freq_get_on_cpu() only when CONFIG_CPUFREQ_ARCH_CUR_FREQ is enabled, and that option is defined only in drivers/cpufreq/Kconfig.x86; otherwise it prints policy->cur = the target passed to cppc_cpufreq_set_target ('freqs.new = target_freq'). The driver then rounds down with cppc_khz_to_perf ('retval = offset + div64_u64(freq * mul, div)'): 1,758,203 kHz -> 87 units = 1,740 MHz, 1,750,000 kHz -> 87 units. So isol.py's cur_khz is a request and not even the exact one; only feedback_ctrs, cpuinfo_avg_freq (busy CPU) or perf stat measure delivery. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/Kconfig.x86 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/acpi/cppc_acpi.c (cppc_khz_to_perf) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/cppc_cpufreq.c (set_target)]

Current upstream arm64 has a boot parameter 'idle=' with 'Format: idle=wfi, idle=yield, idle=nop' (kernel-parameters.txt '[ARM64,EARLY]'; arch/arm64/kernel/idle.c early_param("idle", setup_idle)), where idle=nop keeps idle CPUs out of WFI. The vendor 7.1.3 kernel does NOT have it: its System.map contains cpu_do_idle and arch_cpu_idle but no setup_idle / __setup_setup_idle symbol. So polling idle is not an option on the running kernel, and it would be host-wide (all 128 cores busy) in any case. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/Documentation/admin-guide/kernel-parameters.txt ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/arch/arm64/kernel/idle.c ; host: grep -E ' (setup_idle|__setup_setup_idle|cpu_do_idle|arch_cpu_idle)$' /boot/System.map-7.1.3-arm-agi-20260916-v0.7.2-g4dbc8bb88858 -> only cpu_do_idle, arch_cpu_idle]

Timer-slack facts for Jeremy's device thread: the 50 us default is init/init_task.c '.timer_slack_ns = 50000, /* 50 usec default slack */'; hrtimer_nanosleep() passes current->timer_slack_ns as the expiry range, the timer is not run before its soft expiry and the clock event is armed for the hard expiry (soft + 50 us), so the wake lands about 50 us plus wake-up latency after the requested time unless an earlier interrupt runs the queue; PR_SET_TIMERSLACK (kernel/sys.c) has no capability check, acts on the calling thread only ('current->timer_slack_ns = arg2;'), and is a no-op for RT/DL tasks. A write to /proc/<tid>/timerslack_ns is the alternative. Nothing in this needs root or the governor change. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/init/init_task.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/kernel/time/hrtimer.c ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/kernel/sys.c]

The cpufreq core only re-sends a request when it changes: __cpufreq_driver_target() returns early 'if (target_freq == policy->cur)' unless the driver's CPUFREQ_NEED_UPDATE_LIMITS flag and a pending limits update apply (cppc_cpufreq in master carries that flag). With the performance governor the standing desired_perf of 140 units is written once at the switch and again only when limits change; nothing in the kernel re-asserts it periodically, so a firmware-side reset of the request would be invisible except through the feedback counters. This supports reading feedback_ctrs at both ends of every counted run. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq.c (__cpufreq_driver_target) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/cppc_cpufreq.c (driver flags)]

The proposed positron-cpufreq.service text is valid under systemd 255 as written: systemd expands only '${FOO}' (inside or as a word) and '$FOO' as a separate word, and the unit's '$(seq 1 60)', '$i' and '$c' sit inside one single-quoted word passed to /bin/sh -c; '$$' is the documented spelling for a literal dollar and is the safer form, or the loop can be a root-owned script. The unit's 60 x 1 s wait for policy127/scaling_governor is the correct guard because cppc_cpufreq is a udev-autoloaded module with no systemd ordering target. [https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/255/systemd.service.html (Command lines) ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/cpufreq/cppc_cpufreq.c (MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(acpi, cppc_acpi_ids))]

Reading feedback_ctrs from another CPU is itself a wake-up: counters_read_on_cpu() uses smp_call_function_single() (an IPI that exits WFI) once per counter, so each read from CPU 0 adds 2 IPIs on the target; the idle-window ratio from this check (CPU 123, 1.0 s: ref +125,568, del +175,081 -> 69.7 units = 1,394 MHz) measures mostly the IPI handling itself. On a nohz_full kernel these IPIs would be exactly the disturbance the isolation is meant to prevent, so the run-boundary-only sampling in C4 should be kept and no periodic feedback_ctrs sampler should run during counted runs. [https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/arch/arm64/kernel/topology.c ; host: taskset -c 0 cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu123/acpi_cppc/feedback_ctrs twice]

findings.claim: A busy CPU on the running kernel takes 252-253 arch_timer interrupts per second (the HZ=250 scheduler tick; re-measured 1264 and 1265 in 5 s on CPU 121 at 00:48 UTC, 1261 and 1258 in round3), and only nohz_full can reduce that (to the residual 1 Hz tick plus the task's own timers). On this kernel 'nohz_full=' IS parsed (its handler housekeeping_nohz_full_setup exists in /proc/kallsyms) but is rejected at runtime with the dmesg warning 'Housekeeping: nohz unsupported. Build with CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL', and 'rcu_nocbs=' has no handler at all (rcu_nocb_setup absent), so it would be logged as an unknown parameter; neither has any effect. Also: 'isolcpus=nohz,...' would make the kernel return before applying ANY flag of that isolcpus= setting, so the domain and managed_irq flags would be lost too.

findings.claim: On this kernel a busy CPU receives a function-call IPI for every expedited RCU grace period on the whole host, and such grace periods are triggered by ordinary service activity (a sandboxed systemd service start/stop sets up and tears down a mount namespace): measured on CPU 121 during a 5 s pinned spin, 0 IPIs with nothing else started, 25 IPIs when timedatectl activated systemd-timedated three times, 2 IPIs while idle. isolcpus does not remove this; only nohz_full does, because a task on a nohz_full CPU runs in an extended quiescent state (EQS, 'the kernel need not interrupt it for RCU') and the expedited code skips CPUs in EQS.

Background rate on the 8 CPUs between 23:47 and 00:42 UTC with inspections running: IPI1 on 120-127 rose 123,695 -> 132,061 (8,366 in 55 min = 2.5/s over 8 CPUs).
findings.implication: Even after isolcpus=domain, every hourly fwupd-refresh, every motd-news/ua-timer/apt run, every ssh login (session scope) and every systemd service start on the host sends a few function-call IPIs to the busy pass CPU. One IPI is a short interruption (a few microseconds, not measured here); the lateness band that voids Jeremy's records is 2.5 us (F18), so bursts of these matter. This is the strongest reason to pause the timers (N8) and to apply the reservation rule (N12) even once the CPUs are isolated, and a concrete item that only the rebuilt nohz_full kernel removes.

findings.claim: The managed NVMe queue interrupts on 120-127 are a strict one-queue-per-CPU mapping (nvme0/nvme1 queue_count=129 = 1 admin + 128 I/O queues; /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq has 128 hardware queues; hctx 118..125 map to CPUs 120..127; IRQ nvme0q119..126 and nvme1q119..126 have smp_affinity exactly {120}..{127}). Therefore a queue IRQ on CPU N fires only for I/O submitted from CPU N (blk-mq sends a request to the hardware queue of the submitting CPU, and that queue's vector is affined to that CPU). Writes to /proc/irq/N/smp_affinity for a managed IRQ are refused by the kernel (irq_can_set_affinity_usr() is false for managed IRQs; v6.8 returns EIO 'Input/output error', current mainline returns EPERM; the vendor 7.1.3 errno was not determined). 'isolcpus=managed_irq' has no effect on this host because every such mask contains only one (isolated) CPU; the kernel documentation says exactly this.

'311 127 affinity_hint,nvme0q126,', 'TOTAL irq dirs parsed: 452 with effective affinity touching 120-127: 16', '309 total=22045 on120_127=22045 ... nvme0q124'. kernel-parameters.txt isolcpus= managed_irq: the affinity of managed interrupts 'cannot be changed via the /proc/irq/* interfaces'; the isolation 'is best effort and only effective if the automatically assigned interrupt mask of a device queue contains isolated and housekeeping CPUs'; if a queue's mask holds only isolated CPUs the parameter 'has no effect on the interrupt routing decision' and interrupts 'are only delivered when tasks running on those isolated CPUs submit IO'. kernel/irq/manage.c: 'return __irq_can_set_affinity(desc) && !irqd_affinity_is_managed(&desc->irq_data);' and irq_do_set_affinity(): 'cpumask_and(tmp_mask, mask, hk_mask); if (!cpumask_intersects(tmp_mask, cpu_online_mask))' keep the requested mask. kernel/irq/proc.c v6.8: 'if (!irq_can_set_affinity_usr(irq) || no_irq_affinity) return -EIO;'; mainline master: same test, 'return -EPERM;'.
findings.implication: NVMe interrupts on the pass CPU come only from the SDK's own disk I/O done on that CPU (the churn label writes three 86 MB record files from CPUs 120-127; nvme0q124 on CPU 125 took 22,045 completions). Draft S3's 'fails (EIO/EPERM)' is right in effect; the 'best effort' clause is moot here. irqaffinity=0-119 changes nothing measurable today (no non-managed IRQ is effective on 120-127; 196 are on CPU 0) but is harmless insurance. Keep both flags in the cmdline; they cannot hurt.
findings.action: No kernel setting needed for NVMe. Ask Jeremy to keep the record writer off the pass CPU (write files from a thread on 120-126, or after the timed window). Safe root check after the reboot (writes the same value, so it either errors or changes nothing): echo 120 | sudo tee /proc/irq/176/smp_affinity_list ; expect 'Input/output error' or 'Operation not permitted'.

With isolcpus=domain,managed_irq,120-127 the expected post-reboot workqueue mask is 00ffffff,ffffffff,ffffffff,ffffffff.

Today: phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === background === '--- workqueue cpumask: ffffffff,ffffffff,ffffffff,ffffffff'; host check 'cpumask_isolated=00000000,00000000,00000000,00000000'; 'kernel.timer_migration = 1' (=== sysctl_limits ===).

findings.claim: The no-reboot alternative (a cgroup v2 cpuset isolated partition, P1c) on this kernel updates the domain housekeeping mask at runtime through housekeeping_update(), which flushes the pci-probe, memcg and vmstat workqueues, restricts unbound workqueues, excludes the CPUs from timer migration and re-affines kthreads; it does NOT touch managed-IRQ housekeeping (irrelevant here, N5) and gives no nohz_full. It requires enabling the cpuset controller first (root cgroup.subtree_control has only 'cpu memory pids' today), it is lost on reboot, and the isolcpus 'domain' flag is irreversible at runtime while a partition is reversible.
findings.evidence: phoenix-crb-inspection.txt === cgroups ===: 'subtree_control: cpu memory pids', 'root cpuset.cpus.isolated: ' (empty), 'controllers: cpuset cpu io memory hugetlb pids'. Host kallsyms: 'housekeeping_update' present, 'irq_affinity_adjust' absent. kernel/sched/isolation.c (mainline master) housekeeping_update(): 'int housekeeping_update(struct cpumask *isol_mask)', writes only 'rcu_assign_pointer(housekeeping.cpumasks[HK_TYPE_DOMAIN], trial);', calls 'pci_probe_flush_workqueue(); mem_cgroup_flush_workqueue(); vmstat_flush_workqueue();', 'workqueue_unbound_housekeeping_update(housekeeping_cpumask(HK_TYPE_DOMAIN))', 'tmigr_isolated_exclude_cpumask(isol_mask)', 'kthreads_update_housekeeping()'; 'HK_TYPE_MANAGED_IRQ is never referenced'. kernel-parameters.txt isolcpus= domain flag: domain isolation this way 'is irreversible'; cpusets are recommended for runtime changes.
findings.implication: P1c is a real fallback if the Friday reboot slips: as root, echo +cpuset > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control; mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/isolated; echo 120-127 > /sys/fs/cgroup/isolated/cpuset.cpus; echo isolated > /sys/fs/cgroup/isolated/cpuset.cpus.partition; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/isolated/cpuset.cpus.partition must print 'isolated' (not 'isolated invalid ...'). Jeremy's churn.py reads /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated for core_isolated, and that file reflects isolcpus only, so with the partition path his summary still records core_isolated=false (F19).
findings.action: Prefer P2 (reboot). findings.claim: Seventeen systemd timers and two daemons can disturb a timed run; today all of them can execute on CPUs 120-127 (systemd has no CPUAffinity; PID 1 itself was on CPU 121), after isolcpus they still cost IPIs to the busy pass CPU (N4) and shared L3/DRAM/NVMe bandwidth. The two that change packages and boot files are apt-daily.timer (06:00 and 18:00 UTC plus a 0-12 h random delay, so any time of day; it ran at 21:57 UTC on 21 Oct) and apt-daily-upgrade.timer (06:00 UTC + 0-60 min), which installed kernels linux-image-6.8.0-146 at 06:44 UTC 9 Oct and -147 at 06:16 UTC 15 Oct (with update-initramfs/update-grub/depmod). fwupd-refresh.timer runs HOURLY (*:00 + 0-60 min) and D-Bus-activates the sandboxed fwupd daemon. fstrim.timer fires Mon 26 Oct 00:27:20 UTC (= Sun 25 Oct 17:27 PDT / 20:27 EDT) and will discard most of the 1.7 TB free space on /. The others are light (<1 s to a few s): man-db (daily + 0-12 h, nice 19), motd-news (00:00/12:00 + 0-12 h), ua-timer (6 h), update-notifier-download (24 h), update-notifier-motd (Mon 26 Oct 07:42 UTC), snapd.snap-repair (4x/day; no snaps installed), apport-autoreport (3 h), logrotate and dpkg-db-backup (00:00 UTC daily = 17:00 PDT / 20:00 EDT), sysstat-collect (every 10 min) and sysstat-summary (00:07 UTC), e2scrub_all (Sun 03:10 UTC; no LVM volumes, so a no-op), systemd-tmpfiles-clean (24 h). Automatic reboot by unattended-upgrades is off, and unattended-upgrades.service itself is only the shutdown hook (does nothing while the host runs).

findings.implication: Pausing is one reversible root command set. 'disable --now' removes the timers.target symlinks, so the pause survives the P2 reboot. Because every paused timer has Persistent=true or OnUnitActiveSec, re-enabling after 5 Nov will run the missed jobs immediately, so restore outside a run window. Draft P1b's 'disable unattended-upgrades.service' is unnecessary (it is only the shutdown hook); disabling the two apt timers is what stops package and kernel installs.
findings.action: PAUSE (root, arm account, once, before Oct 23): sudo systemctl disable --now apt-daily.timer apt-daily-upgrade.timer fwupd-refresh.timer man-db.timer motd-news.timer ua-timer.timer update-notifier-download.timer update-notifier-motd.timer snapd.snap-repair.timer apport-autoreport.timer fstrim.timer logrotate.timer dpkg-db-backup.timer sysstat-collect.timer sysstat-summary.timer e2scrub_all.timer ; then verify (any user): systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager (only systemd-tmpfiles-clean should show a NEXT time; keep it, it runs idle-class I/O for <1 s). Optional one-off before the window, outside a run: sudo fstrim -av. RESTORE (after 5 Nov, outside a run window): sudo systemctl enable --now apt-daily.timer apt-daily-upgrade.timer fwupd-refresh.timer man-db.timer motd-news.timer ua-timer.timer update-notifier-download.timer update-notifier-motd.timer snapd.snap-repair.timer apport-autoreport.timer fstrim.timer logrotate.timer dpkg-db-backup.timer sysstat-collect.timer sysstat-summary.timer e2scrub_all.timer. Jeremy's pre-flight can check the pause without root: systemctl is-active apt-daily.timer apt-daily-upgrade.timer fwupd-refresh.timer (expect 'inactive').

findings.claim: Three non-timer background items: (a) netperf.service runs /usr/bin/netserver (pid 1861) since boot; it is idle (0 % CPU) unless someone on the LAN starts a netperf test against this host, which would load CPUs 0-63 via the 64 bnxt_en network queues; (b) smartd (pid 1755, 'smartd -n') polls the two NVMe drives every 30 min (default interval; the --interval line is commented out) through admin commands on queue 0 (CPU 0), milliseconds of work; (c) the sysstat timers fire but collect nothing: /etc/default/sysstat has ENABLED="false" and /var/log/sysstat holds only sa14 and sa15 (14-15 Oct), so sar cannot serve as evidence for the quiet window; cron adds nothing (cron.hourly is empty; every cron.daily script except apport exits under systemd, apport exits unless /var/crash exists).
